text: No new theory in this lesson — four fully worked problems that put the last four lessons to work on fresh numbers, so matrix multiplication, inverses, determinants, and the diagonal shortcut stop feeling like separate topics.

Problem one: for P equals 1,2,0,1 and Q equals 1,0,3,1, compute P Q and Q P. P Q comes out to 7,2,3,1; Q P comes out to 1,2,3,7. They're different — once again, if these were two gates in a circuit, applying them in opposite orders would physically produce different results.

Problem two: find the inverse of N equals 3,2,1,4. Its determinant is 3 times 4 minus 2 times 1, which is 10 — nonzero, so N is invertible. Swapping and negating gives the inverse 0.4, negative 0.2, negative 0.1, 0.3. Multiplying N by that inverse gives exactly the identity matrix, confirming the result.

Problem three: the Pauli-Z matrix is 1,0,0, negative 1. Applying it to ket-one gives negative ket-one — the sign flips. Applying it to ket-zero leaves it completely unchanged. Z doesn't swap basis states the way X did; it leaves ket-zero alone and attaches a negative sign to ket-one, which is why it's called a phase-flip gate rather than a bit-flip gate.

Problem four: for the diagonal matrix D equals 5,0,0, negative 1 and the vector 2,3, the shortcut just scales each entry of the vector by D's matching diagonal entry: 5 times 2 is 10, and negative 1 times 3 is negative 3, giving the result 10, negative 3 — no dot products needed.
Chapter 3 picks up from here with the arithmetic every qubit amplitude actually uses: complex numbers, starting from the fundamentals.
